newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: French troops control Central African oil depot.
newsitem.headline: French troops control Central African oil depot.

text.p: French troops took over Central African Republic's main petrol depot on Tuesday after local army mutineers holding it for three weeks withdrew, witnesses said.
For residents of the capital Bangui, it was the most positive sign that Sunday's truce between mutineers and loyalist troops brokered by four African presidents was holding.
The impoverished country has been paralysed since rebel soldiers seized the depot in the south of the capital at the start of the revolt on November 16, choking fuel supplies.
The depot supplies the entire land-locked country, and filling stations nationwide have been without stock since the start of the mutiny, the country's third this year.
It was not immediately clear how French troops took over the depot, situated in the southwestern part of the city, which remains cut off by rebel barricades.
French troops based in the former French colony under bilateral accords patrol northern Bangui and strategic sites in the city centre. They helped quell a bloody mutiny in May.
Rebels also appear to have handed back state radio's short-wave transmitter outside the capital. The radio resumed broadcasts on Tuesday after operating only on FM since the start of the uprising.

Roadblocks that have come to symbolise the split of the capital into rival ethnic zones remained in place. But the commercial centre which has been largely deserted has started to pick up, with more shops and businesses open.
The presidents of Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon and Mali brokered a 15-day truce to try and avert civil war.
Soldiers, who staged uprisings in April and May over pay and conditions this time demand the resignation of elected President Ange-Felix Patasse.
The mutiny degenerated into ethnic feuding pitting Patasse's northern Baya tribespeople against southern Yakomas who dominate the army and spearhead the revolt.

In a further sign of easing tension, two prominent Yakoma's were buried on Tuesday without incident. Witnesses said former interior minister Christophe Grelombe and his son had been abducted by loyalist troops last Thursday and tortured before being gunned down.
Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoupande was at Bangui's General Hospital when the bodies were transferred from the morgue for burial, witnesses said.

Officials and family members said the burial of former emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa had been further delayed from Tuesday to next week. Plans for a state funeral for the ex-dictator were called off earlier because of the unrest.
They said Bokassa, who died on November 3 of a heart attack, would be buried in his southern ancestral village of Berengo on December 18 in a family ceremony.
